name: U.S. GAO report on federal agency AI implementation and requirements
title: U.S. GAO report on federal agency AI implementation and requirements
answer: This U.S. GAO report reviews how major federal agencies are implementing artificial intelligence. It says 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, but most were still in planning and only about 200 were in current use. GAO found incomplete and inaccurate inventories at many agencies and uneven compliance with federal AI requirements. The most useful point is that agencies have begun implementation, yet key government-wide guidance and management requirements remain unfinished, limiting consistent risk management.

sections.body: The U.S. Government Accountability Office publishes this report page. It is a GAO review of artificial intelligence implementation at major federal agencies. The supplied text is a summary or abstract of the report, not the full report. It examines three questions: agency reported current and planned AI uses, the comprehensiveness and accuracy of agency AI reporting, and agency compliance with selected federal policy and guidance on AI. The text does not state a publication date.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The text says artificial intelligence is rapidly changing the world and could improve government operations, for example by helping agencies analyze drone photos and large datasets, but safeguards are needed to manage AI risks. Federal law and guidance set several requirements for agencies implementing AI, and the text says these have not all been met. There is no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI, which prevents consistent management. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three reported no uses. Reported uses included analyzing camera and radar data to identify border activities, analyzing drone photographs, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Most reported use cases were in planning and not yet in production, with about 200 instances of current use. GAO found incomplete and inaccurate inventory data. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while 15 had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data. Some inventories lacked required elements such as AI life cycle stage or releasability. Two inventories included AI uses later determined not to be AI. Agencies have taken initial steps to comply with requirements in executive orders and federal law, but more work remains. Commerce and GSA fully implemented selected requirements, while OMB and OPM did not fully implement selected requirements, and OSTP did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that 20 of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, and three agencies reported no uses. It states that about 200 instances were current use, while most were in planning. NASA and Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each reported use case, while 15 had incomplete or inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses later determined not to be AI. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all agency-specific AI requirements, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The text also says definitions of AI vary but generally refer to computing systems that learn how to improve their performance.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Government would use this source as a public audit record of what federal agencies report they are doing with AI and where management gaps remain. It gives a government-wide count of reported use cases, shows that most are still planned rather than operational, and identifies incomplete inventories and unmet requirements at OMB, OPM, and OSTP. It is useful for understanding the difference between announced AI activity and production use, and for tracking the requirements that agencies must complete before they can consistently manage AI risks and benefits.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The supplied text is a GAO report summary or abstract, not the full report, so it does not provide detailed methodology, agency-by-agency data, or the full list of use cases. It does not state a publication date. It covers selected federal policy and guidance requirements, not all AI policy, and it relies on agency self-reported inventories, which the text itself says can be incomplete and inaccurate. It does not cover state, local, or private-sector AI use, and it does not evaluate specific AI systems or outcomes.
